messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Fifth protocol. The creature projects fragments of Mirador: a cut radio, an open door, then the egg under white light.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: These are not exactly your memories. Faced with this projection, how do you react?

choices.label: I cut the projection before it changes my memories.
I describe every detail to separate facts from images.
I let it feel the fear without making it carry my guilt.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Eight seconds are missing from your helmet recording. If the creature fills them with your guilt, it may turn that guilt into a survival rule. What do you do with that gap?

choices.label: I stick to the official report until we have proof.
I admit my memory may be false, even if that accuses me.
I search for the source of the radio cut instead of inventing what is missing.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: The creature watches you as if it is waiting for your version of the past. What truth can it receive without becoming trapped in that story?

choices.label: A protected truth: I choose what it can bear.
A complete truth: it has the right to know where it came from.
A verified truth: not one word without corroborated proof.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You are trying to regain control of your memory. I understand, but to it the cut may feel like an order to stay silent.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: That is the best clinical method: name things without concluding too quickly. If it must inherit a memory, let us not hand it a legend.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Few soldiers accept weakening their own report. That caution may keep it from inheriting a false certainty.
